research.title: What does the research say about AI-written code?
research.intro: Four primary sources, each linked below, and every figure quoted from the source rather than summarised second-hand. They disagree with each other in useful ways.

faster.q: Does AI actually make developers faster?
faster.a: Not always. In a 2025 randomized controlled trial, 16 experienced open-source developers predicted AI would cut task time by 24% and afterwards believed it had saved 20%. Measured, the same 246 tasks took 19% longer with AI than without. <link>METR, arXiv:2507.09089</link>

speedup.q: Why do other studies show a large speed-up?
speedup.a: Because they measure different work. A 2023 controlled experiment found developers with GitHub Copilot finished a self-contained HTTP-server task 55.8% faster. That is greenfield code; the 2025 trial used mature repositories the developers already knew well. <link>arXiv:2302.06590</link>

trust.q: How much do developers trust what AI writes?
trust.a: Less every year. In the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, 84% of respondents use or plan to use AI tools, up from 76% in 2024 — yet 46% distrust the accuracy of the output against 33% who trust it, and only 3% highly trust it. Favourable sentiment fell from over 70% in 2023 and 2024 to 60%. <link>Stack Overflow, 2025</link>

wrong.q: Where does AI-generated code actually go wrong?
wrong.a: The same survey ranks the frustrations: 66% cite “AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite”, 45% say debugging AI-generated code takes longer, 20% report losing confidence in their own problem-solving, and 16.3% say it is hard to understand how or why the code works.

secure.a: In a Stanford user study, participants with an AI assistant wrote significantly less secure code than those without — and were more likely to believe their code was secure. Read every generated diff that touches input, auth or secrets against the <owasp>OWASP Top 10</owasp> and the <cwe>CWE Top 25</cwe>. <paper>arXiv:2211.03622</paper>

table.title: How can you check that you actually understood the code?
table.intro: Five things people do after an AI writes a change, compared on what each one actually proves rather than on how thorough it feels.

rows.proves: Nothing you can check later — recognising code reads as understanding it

rows.way: Ask the AI to explain it
rows.proves: That the AI can produce an explanation, not that you followed it

rows.way: Human code review on the pull request
rows.proves: A second person's reading — 45% of developers say reviewing and debugging AI code takes longer
rows.stops: No — it happens after the code exists

rows.proves: The behaviour you thought of; AI-written tests can pass tautologically

rows.way: Answer questions on your own diff (Covate)
rows.proves: Whether you can answer 3 questions about the change you just accepted
rows.stops: Yes — the tool returns HALT_GENERATION until you answer

table.note: The 45% figure is from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey; the Covate row is read from this repository's source, not estimated.

facts.title: What exactly does Covate install and do?
facts.intro: Everything below is read from the open-source repository, so you can check each number against the code before you install anything.

tools.q: What does the MCP server actually add?
tools.a: 4 tools: learning_session (quizzes you on recent changes), debug_search and debug_record (a per-project debugging memory), and term_get (concept lookups across 10 domains). It needs Python 3.11+, binds to 127.0.0.1, and is MIT-licensed.

session.q: How long does one learning session take?
session.a: A session defaults to 3 questions with 4 options each, generated from 7 change-type templates and aimed at 5 focus areas — logic, security, performance, architecture and syntax. The default cap is 10 minutes, configurable from 1 minute to 2 hours.

where.q: Where do the sessions end up?
where.a: On your machine first: the server keeps the 100 most recent sessions per project, and the quiz UI ships in 3 languages. Signing in with GitHub and running the sync client pushes them into the learning ledger, which is free — there is no paid tier anywhere on this site.

assistant.q: Does it work with my assistant?
assistant.a: If your assistant speaks the Model Context Protocol, yes — Claude, Cursor, Copilot and the rest all load MCP servers the same way, described in the <link>2025-06-18 specification</link>.
